catalog_quote: 3.4 Stress patterns. SL has a fixed stress pattern. It is commonly assigned to a penultimate syllable, a characteristic which is typical of Austronesian languages – see e.g. Blust (2013: 251), Nishiyama and Kellen (2007: 11). However, when the penultimate syllable in a disyllabic word contains a schwa, such as gedã [gə.`dã] ‘drum’ and lenga [lə.`ŋa] ‘fall’, stress falls on the ultimate syllable. For a monosyllabic word, stress falls on the full phonological word, in which the vowel tends to be phonologically longer. A stressed syllable is usually marked by a higher pitch, longer duration and greater intensity of the vowel in the syllable. (Kroon 2016:52) ... sources.quote: Solor has words consisting of from one to five syllables. The word accent in words without suffixes usually falls on the penultimate syllable. If this syllable contains a schwa it sometimes falls on the stem-final syllable. When suffixes are added to a stem the accent in by far most cases remains on the originally accented syllable. (Arndt 1937)

sources.quote: 'The general rule is that stress is on the penultimate syllable, but even neighbouring dialects may vary in the details ... Lewoingu [penult], but schwas cannot bear stress there (Nishiyama and Kelen 2007, 11). In Lewolema stress is always penultimate, also if that means a schwa bears the stress, but stress is determined not by the word but by the root, suffixes do not influence it (Pampus 2008, XVI).
